This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 03 - Social Network Analysis](../../Notebooks/Part%2003%20-%20Social%20Network%20Analysis/Part%2003%20-%20Social%20Network%20Analysis.ipynb).
Where the Python version pairs the `atproto` SDK with
[NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), this one pairs
[bskyr](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/) with
[igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) — R's workhorse network library — to
crawl and analyze a *1.5-degree ego network* of follow relationships.

### Learning objectives

* Collect follow and follower lists with `bs_get_follows()`/`bs_get_followers()`.
* Confront the boundary specification problem and sample alters honestly.
* Build a directed igraph from crawled edge lists with node attributes.
* Compute degree distributions, centrality, and Louvain communities.
* Persist a network as edge and node tables and reload it faithfully.

## Setup

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(igraph)
```

As in every part of this series, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks
for credentials (an `atproto.json` file or bskyr's environment
variables), authenticates if it finds them, and sets `bsky_authed`. The
`knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)` line then makes that flag the
default for the whole document: with credentials every chunk runs;
without them the document still knits, but the API chunks are skipped.

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)
```

## 1. The follow-graph endpoints

A follow is a directed tie: `A → B` means A follows B, and B need not
follow back. Two endpoints expose each side of the relation:
[`bs_get_follows()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_follows.html)
([`app.bsky.graph.getFollows`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskygraph/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.graph.getFollows))
returns the accounts an actor **follows** (its "out-edges"), and
[`bs_get_followers()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_followers.html)
([`app.bsky.graph.getFollowers`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskygraph/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.graph.getFollowers))
the accounts that **follow** it (its "in-edges").

Two pieces of vocabulary. An **actor** is the API's word for an account,
identified by handle or DID. And each endpoint has two names because
bskyr wraps an underlying **lexicon** method: the AT Protocol's
[schema language](https://atproto.com/guides/lexicon) formally defines
every endpoint's inputs and outputs, and the linked reference pages are
the authoritative description of what each call accepts and returns.
Both endpoints return at most 100 accounts per request; bskyr follows the
cursors for you when you ask for more (Part 01).

```{r endpoints}
follows_page <- bs_get_follows("nytimes.com", limit = 10)
follows_page |> select(did, handle) |> head(5)

followers_page <- bs_get_followers("nytimes.com", limit = 10)
followers_page$handle
```

Notice that every account comes with two identifiers. The **DID**
("decentralized identifier", `did:plc:...`) is a permanent,
machine-readable identifier that stays with an account for life (see the
[DID specification](https://atproto.com/specs/did)). The **handle**
(`nytimes.com`) is the human-readable name, but
[handles](https://atproto.com/specs/handle) are just domain names and can
change at any time. Throughout this document we build the network on
DIDs and keep handles purely as labels, a habit that pays off in any
longitudinal design: if you revisit a network next year, DIDs will still
match where handles have churned.

A third endpoint, [`bs_get_relationships()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_relationships.html),
checks ties between specific pairs, useful when you need a handful of
edges rather than whole lists (Part 01 used it to measure reciprocity).

### `getKnownFollowers` requires authentication

A fourth graph endpoint,
[`app.bsky.graph.getKnownFollowers`](https://endpoints.bsky.app/#bluesky-app/tag/appbskygraph/GET/xrpc/app.bsky.graph.getKnownFollowers),
returns the followers of an account *that you also follow*: the
"followed by people you know" feature in the app. Because it is defined
relative to **your** follow list, it only works when you are logged in.
bskyr has no wrapper for it, so we build the request with
[httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org/) and attach the session token from
[`bs_auth()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_auth.html),
the same login bskyr uses for every other call. `tryCatch()` turns a
refusal into a message instead of stopping the document:

```{r known-followers}
auth <- bs_auth(get_bluesky_user(), get_bluesky_pass())

known <- tryCatch(
  httr2::request("https://bsky.social/xrpc/app.bsky.graph.getKnownFollowers") |>
    httr2::req_url_query(actor = "bsky.app", limit = 10) |>
    httr2::req_auth_bearer_token(auth$accessJwt) |>
    httr2::req_perform() |>
    httr2::resp_body_json(),
  error = \(e) {
    message("getKnownFollowers was refused: ", conditionMessage(e))
    NULL
  }
)

if (!is.null(known)) map_chr(known$followers, "handle")
```

With your own credentials this lists accounts you follow that also
follow `bsky.app`; an empty result simply means you follow none of them.

## 2. Designing the crawl: boundary specification and sampling

Whole-network analysis needs a *boundary*: who is in, who is out
(Laumann, Marsden, & Prensky 1983). The classic compromise is the **ego
network**: one focal account (the *ego*), the accounts it follows (the
*alters*), and all follow ties *among* them — "1.5 degrees" because we
collect the alters' ties to each other but not their ties to outsiders.

```{r ego}
EGO_HANDLE <- "nytimes.com"

ego_profile <- bs_get_profile(EGO_HANDLE)
ego_did <- ego_profile$did

ego_profile |> select(handle, follows_count, followers_count)
```

### Why sample?

Each alter costs at least one request to enumerate *their* follows. We
sample a fixed number of alters with a fixed seed, trading completeness
for a documented, reproducible budget. The parameters below mirror the
Python notebook's (`N_ALTERS`, `SEED` and `max_pages_per_alter` in its
Section 2 and 3 cells). One thing does *not* carry over: R and Python
have different random number generators, so the same seed (42) draws a
**different** sample of alters in each language. Each sample is
reproducible within its own language, and both are equally valid random
samples, but don't expect the two documents to list the same accounts or
print identical statistics:

```{r sample-alters}
N_ALTERS <- 100              # Python: N_ALTERS = 100
SEED <- 42                   # Python: SEED = 42 (same seed, different generator)
FOLLOWS_PER_ALTER <- 200     # Python: max_pages_per_alter = 2 (2 pages of 100)

ego_follows <- bs_get_follows(ego_did, limit = 4000)

set.seed(SEED)
alters <- ego_follows |> slice_sample(n = min(N_ALTERS, nrow(ego_follows)))

alters$handle |> head(10)
```

## 3. Building the 1.5-degree ego network

The crawl itself: for each alter, fetch up to 200 of their follows, then
keep only those pointing back *into* our node set (`intersect()`). Edges
to accounts outside the boundary are discarded — that is what "1.5
degrees" means. The result of each iteration is a small tibble of
`from → to` pairs, and `list_rbind()` stacks them into one edge list.

We also wrap each fetch in `tryCatch()` because some accounts will be
deleted, suspended, or set to block us, and one bad alter should not
kill a 100-account crawl. But what should a failed crawl *mean*? The
tempting answer, keeping the account as a node with no outgoing edges,
would quietly record "this person follows nobody", a measurement we
never made. Missing data dressed up as an observed zero biases every
statistic below: it lowers density and reciprocity and pushes the
account to the bottom of every centrality ranking. So we record each
failure (with the error message) in `failed_alters`, print it, and
**leave failed alters out of the network**. Our network is "the ego plus
the sampled alters we could crawl", and we report how many we lost:

```{r crawl}
node_set <- c(ego_did, alters$did)
failed_alters <- tibble(did = character(), handle = character(), error = character())

alter_edges <- map2(alters$did, alters$handle, \(did, handle) {
  follows <- tryCatch(bs_get_follows(did, limit = FOLLOWS_PER_ALTER),
                      error = function(e) e)
  Sys.sleep(0.1)
  if (inherits(follows, "error")) {
    reason <- paste0(class(follows)[1], ": ", conditionMessage(follows))
    message("Could not crawl ", handle, " (", reason, "); leaving it out")
    failed_alters <<- add_row(failed_alters, did = did, handle = handle, error = reason)
    return(NULL)
  }
  tibble(from = did, to = intersect(follows$did, node_set))
}) |> list_rbind()

# Drop failed alters everywhere: as nodes, and as targets of others' edges
node_set <- setdiff(node_set, failed_alters$did)
ego_edges <- tibble(from = ego_did, to = setdiff(alters$did, failed_alters$did))
edges <- bind_rows(ego_edges, alter_edges) |>
  filter(from != to, to %in% node_set) |>
  distinct()

G <- graph_from_data_frame(edges,
                           vertices = tibble(name = node_set),
                           directed = TRUE)

c(nodes = vcount(G), edges = ecount(G), alters_not_crawled = nrow(failed_alters))
```

### Node attributes with batched `bs_get_profile()`

[`bs_get_profile()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_profile.html) accepts a vector of actors,
so one call hydrates a whole batch of nodes.

A graph of bare DIDs is hard to interpret, so hydrate every node with
profile attributes, 25 per request (Part 01's batching trick). The
`match()` call lines the profile rows up with igraph's vertex order —
igraph stores vertices in its own sequence, so we must never assume it
matches our tibble's row order. A node whose profile can't be retrieved
(the account vanished between the crawl and this step) gets `NA` from
`match()`, which is exactly right: an unknown follower count is missing,
not zero:

```{r hydrate}
profiles <- map(split(node_set, ceiling(seq_along(node_set) / 25)),
                \(batch) {
                  out <- bs_get_profile(batch)
                  Sys.sleep(0.1)
                  out
                }) |> list_rbind()

idx <- match(V(G)$name, profiles$did)
V(G)$handle          <- profiles$handle[idx]
V(G)$followers_count <- profiles$followers_count[idx]
V(G)$follows_count   <- profiles$follows_count[idx]
V(G)$posts_count     <- profiles$posts_count[idx]

vertex_attr(G, index = ego_did) |> as_tibble()
```

Finally, record when and how the network was collected, a habit from
Part 01: handles change, follows churn, and accounts get deleted, so a
snapshot without a timestamp and parameters can't be reproduced. We also
record which sampled alters we failed to crawl, by DID (the identifier
that doesn't change), so a reader knows exactly which part of the sample
is missing:

```{r crawl-metadata}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
write_json(
  list(ego_handle = EGO_HANDLE, ego_did = ego_did,
       collected_at = format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC",
                             "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
       ego_follows_at_collection = nrow(ego_follows),
       n_alters_sampled = nrow(alters), sampling_seed = SEED,
       follows_per_alter = FOLLOWS_PER_ALTER,
       # sampled alters whose crawl failed, so they are not in the network
       failed_alters = select(failed_alters, did, error)),
  "data/collection_metadata.json", pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE
)
```

## 4. Describing the network

```{r describe}
tibble(
  nodes = vcount(G),
  edges = ecount(G),
  density = edge_density(G),
  reciprocity = reciprocity(G),
  twitter_reciprocity_kwak_2010 = 0.22
)
```

Density is the share of possible directed ties that exist: with $n$
nodes there are $n(n-1)$ possible directed ties, and density is the
share we observed, from 0 (no edges) to 1 (everyone follows everyone).
Reciprocity is the share of ties that are returned: if A follows B, does
B follow A back? Read both against external benchmarks. Density here is
far higher than the platform as a whole (the full Twitter graph Kwak et
al. crawled had a density around $10^{-7}$), because an ego network is,
by construction, a dense pocket of accounts sharing a common anchor.
Then compare the reciprocity with Kwak et
al.'s (2010) figure of about 22% for Twitter at large, shown in the last
column. A newsroom's neighborhood is mostly its own journalists
following one another, so colleagues reciprocate somewhat more often
than Twitter users at large, but most follows still go unreturned: many
staff follow the Times and its star reporters, and those prominent
accounts follow back only a few. Even inside one organization, the
follow graph keeps some of the asymmetry of a news medium. This is a
first concrete lesson that *where you draw the boundary changes the
substantive conclusion*: the same statistic, computed on differently
bounded networks, tells different stories.

### Degree distributions

In a directed follow graph each node has two **degrees**: **in-degree**
(followers within the network, a measure of local audience) and
**out-degree** (follows within the network, a measure of local attention
paid). Note the qualifier *within the network*: an account with millions
of platform-wide followers can have a tiny in-degree here if few of our
sampled alters follow it. One detail surprises almost everyone at first:
the **means of in-degree and out-degree are always identical**, because
every directed edge adds one out-degree to its source and one in-degree
to its target. The *distributions* around that shared mean can still
look very different, and that is what the histograms show:

```{r degrees, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
deg <- tibble(
  did = V(G)$name,
  handle = V(G)$handle,
  in_degree = degree(G, mode = "in"),
  out_degree = degree(G, mode = "out")
)

deg |>
  pivot_longer(ends_with("degree"), names_to = "direction") |>
  ggplot(aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~direction) +
  labs(x = "Degree", y = "Accounts",
       title = "Degree distributions in the ego network") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Degree distributions on social platforms are famously **heavy-tailed**:
most accounts have few connections while a handful have many. The
conventional diagnostic is to plot the distribution on **log-log axes**,
where a heavy tail appears as a slowly decaying, roughly linear scatter:

```{r degrees-loglog, fig.width=6, fig.height=5}
deg |>
  pivot_longer(ends_with("degree"), names_to = "direction") |>
  count(direction, value) |>
  filter(value > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(value, n, color = direction, shape = direction)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Degree", y = "Number of accounts",
       title = "Degree distributions, log-log axes") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Even at this small scale you can usually see the asymmetry: in-degree
stretches further to the right (a few locally prominent accounts collect
many followers within the network), while out-degree is more tightly
bunched, partly a real social pattern and partly because our crawl
truncated each alter's follow list. A caution about vocabulary: a
roughly straight line on log-log axes is *suggestive* of a heavy tail,
not a test of a power law. Rigorous power-law fitting (Clauset, Shalizi &
Newman 2009) needs orders of magnitude more data than 100 nodes.

## 5. Centrality: who matters, and in what sense?

"Importance" in a network is not one thing. Different **centrality**
measures capture different intuitions, and they often disagree in
informative ways:

* **In-degree**: raw audience *within this network*. Simple, local, easy
  to game.
* **Betweenness**: brokerage, the fraction of shortest paths between
  other pairs of nodes that pass through you. High-betweenness accounts
  bridge otherwise separate regions and would fragment the network if
  removed (Granovetter's "weak ties" logic).
* **PageRank**: recursive prestige, where being followed by
  well-followed accounts counts for more. Easley & Kleinberg's
  [Chapter 14](https://www.cs.cornell.edu/home/kleinber/networks-book/networks-book-ch14.pdf)
  gives a gentle derivation.

Kwak et al. (2010) found that on Twitter, follower counts and PageRank
produced very similar rankings, while ranking by retweets surfaced a
*different* set of accounts: "influence" depends on the relation you
measure. One caveat before ranking anyone: **the ego is central by
construction.** We built the network around it, and it follows every
alter, so we drop it from the leaderboard below.
We ask igraph for **normalized** betweenness (`normalized = TRUE`), which
divides by the number of pairs of other nodes, so the scores fall
between 0 and 1 and match what NetworkX reports by default in the Python
notebook. Raw betweenness counts grow with network size, which makes
them hard to compare across networks:

```{r centrality}
centrality <- deg |>
  mutate(
    betweenness = betweenness(G, directed = TRUE, normalized = TRUE),
    pagerank = page_rank(G)$vector
  )

centrality |>
  filter(did != ego_did) |>
  arrange(desc(pagerank)) |>
  select(handle, in_degree, betweenness, pagerank) |>
  head(10)
```

The three rankings agree at the top and diverge below — high-betweenness
accounts that are not high in-degree are the bridges an audience count
would miss.

## 6. Community detection

Do the alters cluster into groups? *Community detection* looks for
partitions of the nodes with many ties inside groups and few between
them. Louvain modularity maximization is the standard fast algorithm; it
is defined for undirected graphs, so we collapse direction first.
*Modularity* (the quality score it maximizes) runs from 0 (no more
internal ties than chance) toward 1 (perfectly separated clusters):

```{r communities}
G_undirected <- as_undirected(G, mode = "collapse")

set.seed(SEED)
communities <- cluster_louvain(G_undirected)

V(G)$community <- membership(communities)

modularity_score <- modularity(communities)

c(n_communities = length(communities),
  modularity = round(modularity_score, 3))
if (modularity_score >= 0.3) "Above the ~0.3 rule of thumb for clear community structure" else
  "Below the ~0.3 rule of thumb for clear community structure"
```

A common rule of thumb reads modularity above about 0.3 as clear
community structure. For this newsroom ego it has come out **below**
that every time we have run the analysis: the network is one interlinked
professional world in which most journalists follow colleagues across
desks, so Louvain's partition describes soft tendencies rather than
sharply separated groups. That is a finding in itself, and it should
temper how strongly we read the communities below.

```{r community-members}
nodes_df <- tibble(
  did = V(G)$name,
  handle = V(G)$handle,
  followers_count = V(G)$followers_count,
  community = V(G)$community
)

nodes_df |>
  add_count(community, name = "community_size") |>
  group_by(community, community_size) |>
  slice_max(followers_count, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  summarise(top_members = paste(handle, collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") |>
  arrange(desc(community_size)) |>
  head(4)
```

Reading a few high-profile members per community usually reveals an
interpretable social context. Here the communities tend to track the
newsroom's beats loosely: politics and Washington reporters often land
together, as do technology and business reporters. With modularity this
low the boundaries are fuzzy, and membership shifts between runs. That interpretive step is yours, not the algorithm's.

## 7. Visualizing the network

A network drawing is a *map*, not a measurement — but it is often the
fastest way to see the community structure we just quantified. The
Fruchterman–Reingold layout pulls connected nodes together; we color
nodes by their Louvain community, size them by in-degree, and label only
the ego. Layouts are random, so `set.seed()` makes the picture
reproducible:

```{r plot, fig.width=11, fig.height=11}
set.seed(SEED)
layout <- layout_with_fr(G_undirected)

plot(G_undirected,
     layout = layout,
     vertex.color = V(G)$community,
     vertex.size = 2 + sqrt(degree(G, mode = "in")),
     vertex.label = ifelse(V(G)$name == ego_did, "ego", NA),
     vertex.label.font = 2,
     edge.color = adjustcolor("gray", alpha.f = 0.3),
     edge.arrow.size = 0,
     main = paste0("1.5-degree ego network of ", EGO_HANDLE,
                   "\ncolored by Louvain community, sized by in-degree"))
```

## 8. Saving and reloading the network

Edge and node tables are the most portable network format:

```{r save}
write_csv(rename(edges, source_did = from, target_did = to),
          "data/edges.csv")
write_csv(nodes_df, "data/nodes.csv")

c(edges = nrow(edges), nodes = nrow(nodes_df))
```

```{r reload}
edges_loaded <- read_csv("data/edges.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
nodes_loaded <- read_csv("data/nodes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

G_loaded <- graph_from_data_frame(
  edges_loaded,
  vertices = rename(nodes_loaded, name = did),
  directed = TRUE
)

c(same_nodes = setequal(V(G_loaded)$name, V(G)$name),
  same_edge_count = ecount(G_loaded) == ecount(G))
```

Any analysis re-runs from disk — e.g., the top PageRank alters:

```{r reload-analysis}
pr <- page_rank(G_loaded)$vector
pr <- pr[names(pr) != ego_did]

tibble(handle = V(G_loaded)$handle[match(names(pr), V(G_loaded)$name)],
       pagerank = pr) |>
  slice_max(pagerank, n = 5)
```

## 9. Research designs with ego networks

What kinds of questions can a design like this answer?

**Ego-network designs.** Long before platform APIs, surveys like the
General Social Survey asked respondents to name the people they discuss
important matters with, producing exactly this structure: an ego,
alters, and alter–alter ties. Classic findings (that ego networks shrank
over time, that they are stratified by education, that kin and non-kin
play different roles) all come from 1.5-degree data. Platform follow
graphs let you collect the same structure for thousands of egos without
a survey, at the cost of measuring "follows" rather than "discusses
important matters with." Granovetter's weak ties and Burt's structural
holes are both statements about ego-network structure that these data
can test at platform scale.

**Homophily.** McPherson, Smith-Lovin, and Cook (2001) summarize one of
sociology's most robust findings: ties form disproportionately between
similar people. With hydrated node attributes you can quantify it here:
do alters in the same Louvain community have more similar follower
counts, account ages, or posting languages than alters in different
communities? On Twitter, Conover et al. (2011) showed homophily at its
starkest: the political retweet network was so segregated that two
communities captured nearly the whole graph.

**Triadic closure.** Networks where your friends tend to be friends with
each other have many closed triangles. Triadic closure is both a theory
of tie formation (you meet friends of friends) and a mechanism platforms
accelerate through "people you may know" recommenders and, on Bluesky,
starter packs. Two standard measurements:
[**transitivity**](https://r.igraph.org/reference/transitivity.html)
(`type = "global"`) is the network-wide share of two-step paths that
close into triangles, and the **average clustering coefficient**
(`type = "localaverage"`) asks, node by node, how connected each
account's neighbors are to one another, then averages. We pass
`isolates = "zero"` so that accounts with fewer than two neighbors count
as zero, which is how NetworkX computes it in the Python version:

```{r triadic-closure}
tibble(
  transitivity = transitivity(G_undirected, type = "global"),
  average_clustering = transitivity(G_undirected, type = "localaverage",
                                    isolates = "zero"),
  density = edge_density(G_undirected)
)
```

Compare both with the density: if ties formed at random with this
density, the chance that two of an account's neighbors are tied would be
about the density itself. Clustering well above it says that ties here
come in closed groups of colleagues, not scattered at random.

**And always: the boundary.** Every number above (density, reciprocity,
centrality rankings, community count, transitivity) is a property of
*the network we specified*, not of "Bluesky." A different ego, a
different sample of alters, a deeper crawl, or follower-based edges
would yield different numbers. Good network papers state their boundary
decision in the first paragraph of the methods section; now you can,
too.

## Ethics and limitations

**Network data is always about third parties.** The ego in this document
is an institution, a newsroom whose public account is part of its
professional output, but the alters, mostly individual journalists, and
the follow relationships among them belong to people who never opted
into a study. They are [public records](https://atproto.com/guides/data-repos)
under the AT Protocol, yet research consistently finds that users are
surprised to learn their public traces are used in research (Fiesler &
Proferes 2018). Practical consequences for your own projects:

* **Minimize.** We stored only DIDs, handles, and aggregate public
  counts: no posts, descriptions, or avatars.
* **Aggregate when reporting.** Prefer community-level and network-level
  statistics over claims about named people, especially low-follower
  accounts.
* **Think before you share edge lists.** A follow network of identifiable
  individuals can reveal affiliations (political, medical, religious)
  that no single profile discloses. A map assembled from thousands of
  public ties creates information that never existed in any one place.
  Consider de-identifying DIDs before publishing, and record your
  collection date so deletions and unfollows can be honored.
* **Boundary specification is also an ethical decision.** Whoever your
  crawl touches becomes a research subject. A seeded sample of an
  institutional ego's follows is a deliberately conservative choice;
  snowballing outward from strangers raises the stakes with every wave.

**Limitations to keep in view:** our per-alter crawl was truncated at the
most recent follows, so within-network edges from prolific followers are
undercounted; the network is a single snapshot of a constantly churning
graph; centrality and community labels describe the crawled graph, not
the people; one ego's neighborhood generalizes to nothing beyond itself;
and Bluesky's user base, early adopters and waves of Twitter migrants, is
not a sample of any broader population.

## Exercises

1. **Change the ego.** Set `EGO_HANDLE` to a different account, such as
   `bsky.app`, and re-run the document from Section 2 onward. Pick an ego
   that follows at least a few hundred accounts so there is something to
   sample, and compare its density and reciprocity to the values above.
2. **Grow (or re-draw) the sample.** Increase `N_ALTERS` to 200 (roughly
   doubling the crawl, still polite) or simply change `SEED` and re-run.
   Which summary statistics stay stable across samples and which jump
   around? This gives you a hands-on feel for sampling error.
3. **Deepen the crawl.** Raise `FOLLOWS_PER_ALTER` from 200 to 500 and
   rebuild the network with the same alters and seed. How many
   within-network edges appear that the shallower crawl missed, and
   which alters contribute them? This quantifies the truncation bias
   discussed in Section 3.
4. **Add a fourth centrality.** Compute closeness centrality
   (`closeness()`) or eigenvector centrality (`eigen_centrality()`), add
   it to the Section 5 comparison, and compute Spearman rank correlations
   among all four measures with `cor(..., method = "spearman")`. Which
   pair disagrees most, and what kinds of accounts drive the
   disagreement?
5. **Reciprocity by community.** For each Louvain community, extract the
   members' subgraph with `induced_subgraph()` and compute
   `reciprocity()` within it. Are ties inside communities more mutual
   than the network-wide rate from Section 4? Interpret your answer in
   light of the news-medium-versus-social-network distinction.
6. **Compare two egos' communities.** Build a second ego network around a
   different institutional ego, run Louvain on both, and compare
   modularity, the number and sizes of communities, and any alters the
   two networks share. Do the shared alters sit in structurally similar
   communities in each network?

## Research project ideas

**1. Homophily across many ego networks.** McPherson, Smith-Lovin & Cook
(2001) argue that homophily is among the most robust regularities in
social life, but most platform evidence comes from a handful of giant
graphs. *Question:* do follow ties on Bluesky cluster by observable
account attributes, and does that clustering vary across egos? *Data:*
30–50 public-facing egos (for example, the members of a public starter
pack), each with a seeded 1.5-degree network built with this part's
pipeline, hydrating attributes such as follower-count tier and account
age. *Method:* Louvain on each network, attribute assortativity with
igraph's `assortativity_nominal()`, and the alignment between
communities and attributes. *Expected challenge:* profile-derived
attributes are noisy proxies, and testing many attributes across many
egos invites false positives, so pre-register which you will test.

**2. How much does the boundary matter? A sensitivity study.** Laumann,
Marsden & Prensky (1983) warned that boundary specification can drive
results, but the warning is rarely quantified for platform data.
*Question:* how sensitive are standard network statistics to
defensible-but-different boundary choices? *Data:* one or two egos,
crawled under systematically varied rules: alters from follows versus
followers, samples of 50/100/200 alters, crawls truncated at 200 versus
1,000 follows per alter. *Method:* density, reciprocity, transitivity,
centrality rankings and Louvain partitions under every condition, with
rank correlations between rankings and partition similarity
(`compare(..., method = "adjusted.rand")`) across conditions. *Expected
challenge:* API calls multiply quickly, so cache every crawl to disk (as
in Section 8), and decide in advance which differences count as "large".

**3. Migration cohorts and community structure.** Bluesky's population
arrived in waves: early invite-code adopters, then surges around
successive Twitter policy shocks. *Question:* do communities in personal
follow networks align with *when* alters joined, a cohort homophily
layered on topical homophily? *Data:* ego networks built with this
pipeline, with each alter's account-creation date from its profile.
*Method:* test whether Louvain communities differ in median join date
(`kruskal.test()`) and whether ties are assortative by join cohort.
*Expected challenge:* creation dates mark when an account was made, not
when a tie formed (the follow endpoints expose no edge timestamps), so
you can establish cohort *clustering* but not the tie-formation
*process*.
